title: Herpes Simplex Virus 2 Associated Mollaret Syndrome Induced by Increased Social Stress—A Case Report and Literature Review
content: Mollaret Syndrome is a form of recurrent aseptic meningitis that is most commonly caused by HSV-2 infection. The symptoms of Mollaret’s Syndrome include headache, neck stiffness, fever and myalgia. Symptoms from recurrent episodes tend to last for 2-7 days without residual neurological symptoms. Common aetiology of Mollaret Syndrome include viral sources but also include autoimmune and iatrogenic causes. Diagnosis can be made utilizing various criteria but is dependent on clinical findings and CSF analysis including microscopy and (polymerase chain reaction) PCR testing. Treatment is limited where antivirals may be trialed to assess any potential benefit in symptom severity, duration and reduction of recurrence though supportive care is the mainstay in treatment. The case presents a 44 year oldwoman of Anglo-Saxon ethnicity presenting with 3 rd presentation of symptoms including headache, chills and myalgia previously diagnosed as HSV-2 associated Mollaret’s syndrome. The patient was diagnosed again with HSV-2 on CSF analysis. The patient was then treated with intravenous acyclovir and then started on prophylactic antiviral therapy. The patient was subsequently discharged without residual neurological deficits. Given the rare presentation of the condition and limited literature, this case report highlights the complexity of Mollaret Syndrome and aids in understanding diagnosis, investigation and management, which may potentially be used within further studies.
